• The lawsuit said the university ​failed to protect its Palestinian members from harassment and targeted them through what it cast as "unfair and biased disciplinary hearings."

• Columbia has previously denied being discriminatory and has condemned hate. Local media reported that it declined to comment ‌on pending litigation. It did ⁠not respond to a Reuters request for comment.

title: University of Michigan changes grade policy for some freshmen
description: The pilot program will apply only to some first-year students at one college.
fullText:
Thousands of freshman students at the University of Michigan will not see letter grades on their report cards next fall.

The school recently announced it is starting a "grade covering" pilot program in 2027 for all incoming first-year students in the College of Literature, Science, and the Arts, for their first semester, where students will only receive pass (P) or no credit (NC) grades instead of A through F letter grades.

Instructors and professors would still assign letter grades for students to know, but students' final GPAs and final transcripts for the first semester would not reflect them.

The school's college, which enrolls about 3,500 first-year students across over 80 majors, said the grade-covering program would benefit students' mental health.

"We believe that covering grades will help students start strong and curb the mental health crisis unfolding among college-aged individuals," the school explained, adding that the change will help "foster an environment where college students can acclimate to the demands of a University of Michigan education and pursue new academic challenges."

The policy change will not apply to other first-year students in the university's other 18 colleges, such as the business or engineering schools.

CDC launches new national campaign to tackle mental health, substance use among teens

Derek Peterson, a professor of history and African Studies and former chair of the university's Faculty Senate, told ABC News he welcomes the new grade policy change for LSA freshmen, some of whom he will be teaching in the fall.

"Mental health is a real problem for undergraduates here in Michigan, as it is across higher education," Peterson said. "Whatever we can do in terms of policy to enable our students to thrive in a difficult and challenging world that bears on their mental health profoundly, I think that's very much the right thing for us to do."

Peterson pointed out that many undergraduate freshmen are navigating new and transitional periods in their young lives, including balancing jobs, moving away from home and societal and familial pressures and the grade policy will enable them to experiment with new classes without the major consequences behind a class failure.

"First-year students are in a particularly precarious position," Peterson said. "The right response is to be charitable, to find ways to work with what our students do know how to do, to give them the space they need to figure it out, so that even if they aren't as well prepared, they can get up to speed in their first year and succeed thereafter."

Meta ordered to pay $567M by New Mexico court over child mental health harm

The University of Michigan declined to comment further on the new policy to ABC News.

The school is not the first higher education institution to implement a grade covering policy. Other schools such as the California Institute of Technology, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Swarthmore College and Wellesley College already have grade covering policies in place for first-year students.

title: The 20 best college towns where life revolves around their universities, ranked
description: College towns offer student experiences that set them apart from big cities. Life in Ann Arbor revolves around the University of Michigan's culture.
fullText:
College towns offer unique student experiences that set them apart from big cities.

For many, large research universities anchor the local economy and culture.

Ann Arbor tops the list of best college towns, driven by the University of Michigan's rich culture.

For many students, college is a time filled with rigorous classes, internship applications, and energy-drink-filled all-nighters.

College towns often offer a unique experience that helps these students manage flourishing social lives and hobbies alongside their academic careers.

Business Insider looked at some of the cities and towns across America where students can thrive, and compiled a list that best matches the loose definition of a college town.

To do so, we used data from the Census Bureau's latest population estimates and from WalletHub's 2025 ranking of the best college towns. We then filtered out major cities, focusing instead on places where colleges and universities anchor the local economy and lifestyle.

Not all college towns are built the same, however, and while some are extensions of nearby metropolises, others are smaller communities tucked away from other urban areas.

School: Brigham Young University

Nestled between mountains in the Utah Valley, the city of Provo is home to the private Brigham Young University, which has a student population of over 35,000 students.

The town has a lively economy, a young population, and its local culture is closely tied to religion and sports. Locals often enjoy the city's unique access to hiking trails and stunning natural landscapes.

School: University of Tennessee — Knoxville

Home to the University of Tennessee — Knoxville and its over 40,000 students, the city of Knoxville is a vibrant and energetic community.

The city is considered a gateway to the Great Smoky Mountains — as it's located less than an hour away from unique Appalachian landscapes — and a hub for country music, which soundtracks the city's scene.

During gamedays, over 100,000 fans pack into the school's Neyland Stadium in their best orange-and-white attire.

Located between Austin and Houston, College Station, Texas, is one of the state's best college towns. The city's culture, economy, and lifestyle are shaped by Texas A&M University.

The land-grant, SEC university has one of the largest student populations at its College Station campus, with over 72,000 students.

School culture unites the city, with Aggie pride inescapable on gamedays as fans congregate at the school's Kyle Field, which seats over 100,000.

The city is also home to the George H.W. Bush Presidential Library and Museum.

17. Chapel Hill, North Carolina

School: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill

The school's roughly 34,000 students shape local culture and economy. Along with Durham — home to Duke University — and Raleigh — home to North Carolina State University — Chapel Hill is part of North Carolina's Research Triangle, a region where tech and education are among the most popular fields of employment.

Thanks to the college's prevalence and the region's entry-level job opportunities, the town has a highly educated, uniquely young population.

School: Michigan State University

Neighboring the state capital of Lansing, the city of East Lansing combines college culture with government employment.

The city is home to roughly 52,000 students at Michigan State University, which dominates local culture and sports. The school's sprawling campus sits directly across the city's downtown. Restaurants, cafés, shops, and bars cluster around the university.

15. San Luis Obispo, California

School: California Polytechnic State University.

Halfway between San Francisco and Los Angeles, the town of San Luis Obispo combines the energy of a college town with the laid-back lifestyle of California's Central Coast.

The over 20,000 students at Cal Poly have easy access to the region's beaches, mountain trails, and wine country, while the city's compact downtown is filled with restaurants, shops, and nightlife.

School: University of Connecticut

Population: 15,979 (per the 2020 census)

In the small community of Storrs, which is surrounded by the forests and farmland of northeastern Connecticut, the University of Connecticut is the center of life.

Downtown Storrs, located next to campus, has more than 70 businesses, as well as nature preserves and hiking trails. The university's size gives the otherwise rural community a steady stream of restaurants, events, arts programming, and student activity, especially during UConn basketball game days.

School: Harvard University, Massachusetts Institute of Technology

Few American cities have an academic identity as strong as Cambridge. With Harvard and MIT anchoring higher education in the city, the opportunities available attract thousands of students, researchers, and academics from around the world.

Harvard Square mixes restaurants, shops, museums, and entertainment around Harvard's historic campus, while Kendall Square, beside MIT, has become a hub for jobs in technology, biotechnology, and startups.

The city's location across the Charles River from Boston also gives students easy access to the metropolis's jobs, nightlife, and culture via public transit.

The University of Georgia's historic campus sits directly across from downtown Athens, making the city one of the most recognizable college towns in the South.

Athens has a prominent music scene that produced famous bands like R.E.M. and the B-52s, and live music remains a major part of the city's identity. Its walkable downtown is packed with local restaurants, bars, coffee shops, boutiques, and music venues.

On fall weekends, Georgia Bulldogs football takes over the city as tens of thousands of fans pack Sanford Stadium.

School: Washington State University

Tucked among the rolling hills of southeastern Washington, Pullman is a small town where Washington State University defines local culture and identity.

The compact downtown is within walking distance of campus and has many locally owned restaurants, coffee shops, and retailers.

The city's remote location contributes to a close-knit student and faculty community. School traditions and Cougar sports play a major role in local identity, which is also influenced by the natural landscape that surrounds the city.

School: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign

The University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign spans the neighboring cities of Champaign and Urbana and is home to one of the Midwest's largest college communities, with over 59,000 students.

The university's research focus also extends to the local economy, with its Research Park and business incubator supporting technology companies and startups, and drawing students to remain in the area for internships and jobs long after graduation.

Located on Wyoming's high plains between mountain ranges, Laramie combines a historic Western downtown with the culture of the state's flagship university.

The over 10,000 students at the University of Wyoming have easy access to hiking, mountain biking, climbing, skiing, and other outdoor activities in the surrounding mountains and forests.

The city's downtown adds restaurants, coffee shops, breweries, and local businesses within a relatively compact area near campus, and the college culture also spans museums, performing arts, and Wyoming Cowboys athletics.

Purdue University's large student body of nearly 58,000 makes West Lafayette one of the most university-driven communities in the Midwest.

The school's reputation in engineering, science, and technology contributes to a local economy centered on research and innovation, while Big Ten athletics give the city's culture a strong sense of school spirit.

School: University of California, Berkeley

UC Berkeley's academic reputation and history of student activism have helped shape the city's culture for generations.

Just south of campus, Telegraph Avenue remains one of the city's most distinct student districts, with streets lined with independent stores, restaurants, and record shops.

Students can also head into the Berkeley Hills to explore beautiful trails and parks or easily reach San Francisco and other Bay Area communities through public transportation.

School: University of Wisconsin—Madison

Built between two lakes, Madison gives students a unique mix of a major state capital, a large Big Ten university, and easy access to the outdoors.

The city's State Street serves as the main connector between campus and the Wisconsin State Capitol, with cafés, restaurants, bars, galleries, and shops lining the corridor. On warm days, students gather along Lake Mendota at the university's Memorial Union Terrace.

College sports, cycling, lake activities, farmers markets, and a strong local food scene keep the city lively year-round.

Schools: Florida State University, Florida A&M University

Florida's capital city has one of the largest and most varied student communities on this list, anchored by multiple public colleges.

Florida State University and Florida A&M University each bring distinct traditions to the city, and along with the local Tallahassee State College, the city has a student population of over 65,000.

FSU's Seminoles generate major football weekends around Doak Campbell Stadium, while FAMU, one of the country's most prominent historically Black universities, has its own deep academic, cultural, and athletic traditions.

The city is also the center of the Florida state government and offers plenty of opportunities for students interested in politics, public policy, law, and government.

Located in the center of North Florida, Gainesville is home to the University of Florida's over 63,000 students, along with thousands of researchers, Gators fans, and university employees who give the city a unique college-town identity.

The city is surrounded by nature preserves, forests, and freshwater springs where locals can swim, kayak, and tube, while the downtown area has a growing restaurant, craft beer, and arts scene that keeps students busy year-round.

College football is especially important to local culture, with home games drawing dozens of thousands of fans to the school's Ben Hill Griffin Stadium throughout the fall.

The University of Virginia shapes Charlottesville's deep academic and historic identity, while the surrounding Blue Ridge foothills give the city easy access to some of Virginia's most scenic landscapes.

The university's campus sits near a lively corridor of restaurants and shops, while the pedestrian Downtown Mall serves as a center for dining, shopping, and live entertainment.

The surrounding region is also known for its unique wineries, farms, and natural mountain scenery.

School: Arizona State University

Arizona State University's sprawling Tempe campus gives the city a distinctly youthful energy within the larger Phoenix metropolitan area.

Historic Mill Avenue, directly beside campus, is lined with restaurants, bars, shops, and entertainment venues, becoming a major center of student activity at night.

The school's focus on research, technology, and entrepreneurship also bolsters Tempe's economy, while the city's location within the Phoenix metro area gives graduates access to one of the Southwest's largest job markets.

School: University of Michigan-Ann Arbor

Home to the University of Michigan and its over 50,000 students, Ann Arbor is the best and most distinct college town in the US.

College culture is deeply woven into the city's landscape, where campus buildings blend into a walkable downtown filled with restaurants, bookstores, cafés, bars, and cultural institutions.

Few traditions dominate the city like Michigan football, which attracts over 100,000 fans to Michigan Stadium during fall Saturdays, while maize-and-blue crowds fill the surrounding streets and businesses.

The unique combination of college sports, a lively downtown, a major research university, and a strong cultural scene makes Ann Arbor one of the country's quintessential college towns and ranks it at the top of this list.

title: Appetite-suppressing hormone may protect liver from inflammation
description: Researchers at McMaster University have discovered that a naturally occurring hormone best known for suppressing appetite and promoting weight loss also helps protect the liver from inflammation through a previously unknown signaling pathway, opening new possibilities for treating advanced fatty liver disease.
fullText:
edited by 
 Gaby Clark, reviewed by Robert Egan

Researchers at McMaster University have discovered that a naturally occurring hormone best known for suppressing appetite and promoting weight loss also helps protect the liver from inflammation through a previously unknown signaling pathway, opening new possibilities for treating advanced fatty liver disease.

The findings, published in Cell Metabolism on Aug. 10, 2026, reveal that the hormone GDF15 can suppress liver inflammation and slow the progression of liver scarring independently of weight loss—a surprising discovery that challenges longstanding assumptions about how the hormone works.

Millions of people worldwide live with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), a severe form of fatty liver disease that can progress to cirrhosis, liver cancer and liver failure. While new weight-loss medications have improved outcomes for many patients, liver inflammation often persists even after significant weight loss. The new research identifies a biological pathway that helps regulate liver inflammation, suggesting future treatments may be able to complement existing weight-loss therapies.

"Our findings show that GDF15 does much more than regulate appetite and body weight," says Gregory Steinberg, professor in McMaster University's Department of Medicine, co-director of the Centre for Metabolism, Obesity and Diabetes Research (MODR) and senior author of the study. "We discovered that GDF15 activates a natural brain-to-liver signaling pathway that helps suppress liver inflammation and reduce fibrosis. This changes how we think about the hormone and suggests it may be part of the body's own defense system against chronic liver injury."

Using mouse models that closely mimic human MASH, researchers combined genetic, pharmacological, genomic and spatial transcriptomics approaches to investigate the role of GDF15 in advanced liver disease. They found that GDF15 activates signaling from the brain through the nervous system, leading to the release of glucocorticoids, a class of steroid hormones that play a vital role in metabolism, immune function and the stress response.

The glucocorticoids help dampen inflammation in the liver, and these protective effects occur independently of changes in food intake, body weight or liver fat. GDF15 was also found to help limit the progression of liver fibrosis, a buildup of scar tissue associated with advanced disease.

"GDF15 helps reprogram liver cells to reduce inflammation and scarring using advanced spatial technology," says Dongdong Wang, first and corresponding author of the study and assistant professor in McMaster's Department of Medicine. "Instead of causing liver damage, GDF15 appears to help calm the liver's immune system. It shifts immune cells into a more protective and less active state, helping reduce inflammation and prevent damage to the liver."

Research published in 2023 by Steinberg and Wang showed that GDF15 helps maintain calorie burning during weight loss, but the new study reveals an entirely different role for the hormone: protecting the liver through a previously unknown anti-inflammatory pathway.

Together, researchers say the two studies could help guide the development of future therapies aimed specifically at liver inflammation, a major driver of disease progression that remains difficult to treat.

Steinberg, an executive member of NexusHealth at McMaster and chief scientific officer, shareholder and co-founder of Espervita Therapeutics, recently co-authored preclinical research describing a promising drug candidate for advanced liver disease. While that work focused on a potential therapeutic compound, the new study identifies a biological pathway the body naturally uses to suppress liver inflammation, offering new insight that could inform the next generation of treatments.

"Current therapies largely focus on reducing body weight and liver fat," says Steinberg. "Our work suggests there may be value in combining those approaches with therapies that directly target inflammation. By understanding how the body naturally protects the liver, we can identify new opportunities to develop more effective treatments for people living with MASH."

Dongdong Wang et al, GDF15 suppresses liver inflammation independently of weight loss through neuroendocrine glucocorticoid signaling, Cell Metabolism (2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.cmet.2026.07.008

title: Forget DeepSeek. China’s real ‘Sputnik moment’ is happening on campus as American universities lose their advantage
description: China's tech rise runs deeper than any single breakthrough. Its universities generate critical technology patents at 8x the U.S. rate
fullText:
When DeepSeek unveiled an AI model last year that rivaled America's best at a fraction of the cost, or when a Chinese hypersonic missile test caught U.S. intelligence off guard to the point where a top U.S. general called it "very close" to a "Sputnik moment", the reaction each time was the same: that a handful of Chinese firms had suddenly pulled ahead.

What role do Chinese universities play in critical technology patents?

What impact are U.S. research funding cuts having?

How does Chinese patent quality compare to U.S. patents?

Why are sanctions on Chinese firms potentially ineffective?

But a sweeping new National Bureau of Economic Research study of nearly 14 million Chinese patents suggests that framing misses the real story—and it's a more unsettling one for the United States.

Harvard Business School's Josh Lerner and his co-authors dug into who is actually filing the patents behind the 14 technology areas the Pentagon deems critical—advanced computing, space technology, AI, hypersonics and biotech. The answer: Chinese universities account for more than a quarter of the country's inventions in those fields, 8x the U.S. rate at 3.3%, with state-owned enterprises and the government accounting for just 4%.  Fewer than one in 10 Chinese critical technology patents involve an inventor with U.S. work experience, undercutting the assumption that Beijing relies on returning U.S. talent for innovation.

Lerner told Fortune his team was "programmed" to expect a few large corporations like Huawei and Tencent to lead the charge on Chinese innovation through patents similarly to IBM and Samsung in the U.S. Instead, they found Chinese innovation in critical technologies "much more diverse—spread out across the parties," with universities "more represented" there than anywhere else in the country's patent system. That's a reversal of the U.S. pattern, where academic patenting is "more of a sideshow."

"We've clearly seen this dramatic boom in terms of research funding and patenting in China," Lerner said, "and the natural question being is this bearing fruit? In the software side, Deepseek was certainly something that was really not anticipated, and clearly these open-source Chinese models are getting an enormous amount of traction."

The findings arrive as the quality gap many assumed would protect American tech leadership seems to be closing, with DeepSeek, Moonshot and Z.AI going toe-to-toe with U.S. frontier labs and beating them on cost.

Using four text-based measures of patent novelty and scientific relevance, the authors found no evidence China's patent boom came at the cost of quality—Chinese patents have converged with, and in some technologies overtaken, their U.S. counterparts. The share of Chinese critical-technology patents containing "disruptive" technical language jumped from under 2% in the early 1990s to 16% by 2022, closing in on the American share of roughly 20%.

title: Indian national accused of Arizona girlfriend's murder entered US on student visa: federal sources
description: Varun Batchigari allegedly strangled Julissa Salazar near the University of Arizona, then boarded a flight to India before the FBI had him arrested.
fullText:
The man accused of murdering his teenage girlfriend in Arizona allegedly tried to cover his tracks, flee the country and vanish overseas.

Federal law enforcement sources told Fox News the accused killer, 20-year-old Varun Batchigari, is an Indian national who entered the United States through Los Angeles International Airport on Jan. 8, 2024, on an F-1 student visa.

After the alleged killing, authorities say Batchigari boarded a flight from Houston bound for India with a layover in Germany, where he was arrested after the FBI alerted local authorities.

Migrant Who Fled Ireland After American Mother's Murder Is Arrested In Jordan

The FBI is now working to extradite him back to Arizona to face a first-degree murder charge.

Batchigari is charged with murdering his 19-year-old girlfriend, Julissa Salazar, who Tucson police say was strangled Thursday inside an off-campus apartment near the University of Arizona.

Investigators allege Batchigari stole Salazar's cellphone and credit cards after the killing, then sent a series of text messages to her mother while posing as the victim in an apparent attempt to conceal the crime. The messages raised concern among Salazar's family, prompting a welfare check that led officers to discover her body.

A felony warrant paints a picture of escalating violence, a deteriorating relationship and mounting personal troubles in the months leading up to Salazar's death.

Fitness Trainer Told Friend She Was 'Scared For Her Life' Weeks Before Body With Matching Clothing Found

According to the warrant, obtained by KOLD-TV, Batchigari had previously been involved in an assault case investigated by the University of Arizona Police Department.

Witnesses interviewed by investigators said Salazar moved out after experiencing problems with Batchigari in late 2025 and had planned to end the relationship because of an alleged history of domestic violence.

The warrant also includes allegations from multiple witnesses describing prior violent behavior. One witness told investigators Batchigari sexually assaulted her at a Halloween party but said she never reported the allegation to law enforcement.

Another witness told investigators Batchigari had been expelled from the University of Arizona following a fight and later lost his job, leading to financial problems and concerns about his student visa status and ability to pay rent.

Exclusive: Dhs Seeks Custody Of Illegal Immigrant Charged With Murder After Trump Deportation, Biden Release

Federal records reviewed by Fox News show Batchigari remained in lawful immigration status at the time of the alleged murder despite his reported expulsion from the University of Arizona.

Because international students on F-1 visas are generally required to remain enrolled to maintain their legal status, it is unclear why his immigration status had not yet changed.

A Tucson Police Department spokesperson told Fox News Digital there were no updates beyond the information already released publicly. Fox News Digital also reached out to the University of Arizona to confirm Batchigari's enrollment history and whether Salazar was a student, but did not immediately receive a response.

"Processing wild/game animals in community kitchens is strictly prohibited," the school's new policy states.

title: Teaching Coding When AI Can Write the Code
description: Now that AI can write code, a student's submission no longer shows what they really understand. Here, I share three approaches we're testing at the University of Texas at Austin.
fullText:
Now that AI can write code, a student's submission no longer shows what they really understand. Here, I share three approaches we're testing at the University of Texas at Austin.

For as long as we’ve taught programming, the student’s code has provided a window into the students’ thinking. Errors, the code structure, the awkward working solution—all of it showed how someone reasoned and where they got stuck.

It was never a clean window. Students have always copied, crammed, and borrowed, sometimes turning in work they didn’t fully understand. But the code still left clues. Generative AI has changed that: A finished program now tells us more about a student’s prompts than their ideas. And here’s the part that should unsettle us—often, the better the code looks, the less we can say about what the student actually learned.

This raises a bigger question: If AI can write code, should we still teach coding? I believe the answer is yes, at least for some students and situations. But that’s another topic. Here, I want to focus on the next step: If we continue teaching coding in a world with AI, how can we know if students are really learning?

Some schools have responded by trying to catch students. They use AI detectors, surveillance tools, locked-down browsers, stricter rules, and clearer honor codes. This has also led to more suspicion.

Some of these responses make sense. Teachers want to protect learning, and schools want to keep things fair. But using detection as the main way to assess students is weak. Stanford researchers found that popular AI detectors often falsely flagged writing by nonnative English speakers, with 61.22% of TOEFL essays in one study marked as AI-generated. OpenAI even retired its own AI Text Classifier in 2023 because it wasn’t accurate enough. If the company that created the tool can’t reliably detect AI, it’s probably not a good idea to base your honor code on it.

But detection isn’t the real issue. Even if we had a perfect detector, we’d still be asking the wrong question. Instead of asking, “How do we stop students from using AI?” we should ask, “How do we teach coding in a world with AI, making use of its benefits, while still being able to see if students are learning?”

We’re seeing this challenge with students at AET, the Arts and Entertainment Technologies Department at the University of Texas at Austin. Although my usual home is Computer Science, it so happens that AET is within the College of Fine Arts at UT, which offers many other ways to learn and assess: studio work, critique, rehearsal, revision, and performance.

In the arts, the final piece has never been the whole story. A painting doesn’t explain the choices behind it. A performance doesn’t reveal the rehearsals. A design board doesn’t show the discarded versions. A composition doesn’t tell you where the student struggled or what they finally learned to hear.

Art education has developed practices that focus on visible progress. Students bring in sketches and drafts, discuss influences, revisions, and failures, and rehearse, perform, and critique each other’s work while it’s still in progress.

At AET, we teach creative coding, which means programming to create art, design, games, or experiences. That doesn’t mean coding for poets. Our students—game designers, web developers, and programmers—start from scratch and learn advanced concepts in tools like Processing and p5.js. In the creative coding tradition, a program is often called a sketch, borrowing the term from the art world. It means something temporary, exploratory, and open to change—something you make, test, revise, and share.

So in creative coding, we were already leaning toward the studio model of sketches, experiments, iterations, and critique. Now we’re pushing that further as we rethink how we teach coding in an AI world. Here are three things we’re already using or actively developing.

We run the class like a studio. It’s not that work never happens at home, but the most important work needs to be seen in the classroom. Students show their code, including false starts, revisions, the choices they made, and the reasons behind them. Assignments are no longer just things you submit—they become projects you develop in public.

AI isn’t banned from the classroom. Instead, it’s treated as a helpful assistant to learn from. Students share prompts and techniques. They use AI, Google, Stack Overflow, classmates, or any other resources.

But you still need to take responsibility for your work. If you submit or present it, you must explain what the code does, why you made those choices, and how it works. If I need to ask your AI to understand your code, something is wrong. Getting help is fine, but hiding behind that help is not.

You can’t outsource to AI what the whole room watched you build.

A real studio needs students talking out loud together in the room every day. This also helps with another issue that isn’t about AI. Many people say students today are quieter than in the past. While this is mostly based on stories rather than long-term studies, these stories are common and consistent. Faculty on all types of campuses talk about silent classrooms and students who hesitate to speak up, especially since 2020.

Whatever the reason, this silence can be changed, and the solution is the same as for AI challenges: encourage students to participate. Communication is one of the most important skills in any career, including explaining ideas, defending choices, and persuading others in real time. Students don’t develop these skills by just submitting AI-guided work online. When they share their work publicly, it not only prevents AI misuse but also helps them build the skills they need most.

We know the usual pattern: A student asks, AI answers, and the student copies. We’ve tried to invert this. In our new approach, the AI works with the student on a set of topics, engages them in a conversation they must navigate, and ultimately assesses how well they understand the material, which leads to a grade.

This idea has a research background that goes back before ChatGPT. Teachable-agent systems like Betty’s Brain showed that explaining—even to a software agent—forces students to organize their knowledge, make connections clear, and find gaps. Our model uses this insight differently. The student isn’t teaching the bot. Instead, the student is having a conversation with it, learning, discussing, debating, and showing what they understand.

How did we do this? With fairly simple prompt engineering, we created an avatar chatbot of Vera Molnár (1924–2023), a pioneer of algorithmic art. The bot takes on Molnár’s role, drawing students into conversations about randomness, computation, generative art, and creative choices. Her practice sits exactly where creative coding students need to think: between rule and variation, system and choice, computation and visual judgment.

A system prompt sets the topics and types of questions to ask. The bot goes through these with the student, asks for more detail on unclear answers, and keeps following up until there is proof of understanding. At the end, it reviews the conversation against a rubric, giving us a clear record of which ideas the student covered, where they struggled, and how well they improved.

Besides the assessment, which is often accurate, the transcript becomes a different kind of proof, showing what a typical assignment might hide. What did the student notice? What did they misunderstand? Could they connect the concept to the code? Could they defend their choices? Could they revise their explanation when challenged?

When we switch the roles, something surprising appears: the one thing a finished submission can’t show.

Programming has never really had a tradition of performance. Musicians have it, painters have it, and dancers have it. Live coding is starting to change that.

Every semester at AET, students from different disciplines stage an algorave together—short for algorithmic rave. Audio sets, projection pieces, game demos, lasers, drones, experience design. The creative coding class brings live visuals into the live-coding tradition: Code is written and modified in real time, the screen is projected, and the audience watches the editor change as the visuals respond to the music other students are playing.

No prerender. No hiding the machinery.

The Live Coding manifesto, written in 2004 by TOPLAP, includes a line that fits every AI-era assessment conversation: “Obscurantism is dangerous. Show us your screens.” This is not just a performance ethic; it’s also an assessment strategy.

A student walks on stage. The projected screen is their editor. The room can read it. The music starts. And they build up a line of code on screen like:

osc(18, 0.08, 1.2)

 .modulate(noise(3), 0.25)

 .rotate(() => time * 0.1)

 .out()

This is JavaScript building visuals in real time. FFTs, chained functions, higher-order manipulations. When you’re manipulating code like that on stage, you’d better know what you’re doing.

AI can help you prepare. Good. Let it.

But once you’re on stage, the question shifts from “Can you copy and paste code?” to “Can you control it?” You can paste code into a file, but you can’t paste your way through three minutes of public debugging while the whole projection turns into a beige rectangle. In a live build, understanding has nowhere to hide.

Can you read the code, make changes on purpose, and recover when something unexpected happens? That’s fluency: knowing what to do next while the system is still running.

It is very hard to plagiarize panic.

So far, our results are based on our own observations. We haven’t conducted a controlled study or compared different groups, so what we have seen might just be early variation rather than patterns that apply more broadly. For now, these efforts are experiments, not final answers.

Assessment in studio and live performance settings is always subjective and focused on people. It relies on monitoring students’ progress, providing feedback, and observing how they handle challenges. We do not plan to change this core approach.

For the Molnár conversation assignment, students discussed Molnár using an AI system. The AI then created a summary and analysis of each student’s understanding. Teaching assistants reviewed this analysis, conducted their own assessments, and assigned grades. In our small experiments, the AI’s assessments using the rubric matched closely with the teaching assistants’ own evaluations.

We also used AI to help grade the end-of-term coding assignment. In this project, students improved an object-oriented game by adding strategies like heuristics, search algorithms, and learned behaviors. Since our teaching assistants had limited experience with object-oriented programming, we developed a detailed rubric and had an AI model use it to evaluate each submission. The AI’s analysis was given to the teaching assistants as support. It helped them see how each project was structured, spot important OOP design choices, and use the rubric with more confidence. The teaching assistants still made their own grading decisions. I was available as the OOP expert for any questions they could not answer. From what I observed, this substantially helped the teaching assistants understand and grade the students’ OOP design work.

More broadly, both approaches appear to enable substantive feedback at a scale that would otherwise be difficult given our current student-to-teaching-assistant ratios.

We spent the first two years of the generative AI panic asking how to catch students using AI—or prohibit it altogether. Wrong question.

The real question is whether the assignment gives students a real way to show and develop their understanding. This view isn’t limited to educators. NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang recently argued that students should not focus on finding an “AI-proof” subject. Instead, he suggested they consider how AI can help them learn more deeply and develop their skills and sense of purpose. He highlighted storytelling, creativity, design, and judgment as abilities that will stay important even as AI takes over more tasks. This supports a key idea in coding education: The aim is not to prove you didn’t use any tools, but to help students show how they think, make choices, revise, and take responsibility for their work.

These three practices are experiments, not universal solutions. They work especially well in creative coding, where code already has a public, visual, and performative aspect. But they suggest a broader principle: As finished work becomes easier to generate, assessment needs to focus more on process, explanation, revision, and mastery.

This matters outside of school too. A polished memo no longer proves there was real thinking behind it. A working prototype no longer proves product sense. A passing pull request no longer proves the developer made the change carefully and thoughtfully. AI makes production easier, so evaluation must focus more on how people think, choose, revise, and recover—in code review, hiring, and performance management. The artifact is no longer the proof. The process is.

Generative AI didn’t make assessment impossible. It just made a hidden weakness obvious. We were putting too much trust in finished work. The arts always knew better.

title: Ole Miss football legend Archie Manning will get statue on campus
description: Ole Miss football legend Archie Manning will be honored with a statue on campus by the Manning Center, Ole Miss said.
fullText:
OXFORD — Ole Miss football legend Archie Manning will be getting a statue outside the Manning Center.

An Ole Miss spokesperson confirmed the news to the Clarion Ledger on Aug. 8, and said the school will have more information in the coming days.

Manning, 77, is one of the most revered figures in the history of the Ole Miss program. He was the star quarterback for Ole Miss from 1968-70 under coach Johnny Vaught. Manning also played baseball at Ole Miss.

Manning ended his Ole Miss career with 56 touchdowns, which was a school record, and 5,576 yards of total offense. He finished No. 3 in Heisman Trophy voting in 1970. He was a 1989 inductee into the College Football Hall of Fame and was drafted No. 2 overall by the New Orleans Saints in the 1971 NFL Draft.

Additionally, Manning is the father of NFL greats Peyton Manning and Eli Manning. Eli played for Ole Miss from 2000-03 and was third in Heisman Trophy voting in 2003. Archie Manning now runs the Manning Passing Academy with his sons.

Archie's grandson, Arch, is the quarterback for Texas and considered a frontrunner for the Heisman Trophy.

The Manning patriarch has already been honored on the Ole Miss campus in other ways. Speed limit signs on campus are 18 miles per hour, which is a nod to Archie's number for the Rebels. Ole Miss football practices in the Olivia and Archie Manning Athletics Performance Center.

Manning is the second Ole Miss football player to be honored with a statue. Chucky Mullins has a movable bust that is prominently featured on football game days in the Ole Miss tunnel. Mullins was paralyzed in a 1989 game and died in 1991 due to complications from the injury.

Vaught, Coolidge Ball and Tim Elko are other Ole Miss athletic statues on campus.

Vaught is Ole Miss' winningest football coach with 190 victories, and his statue was dedicated in 2008.

Ball was the first Black athlete at Ole Miss, playing basketball from 1971-74. His statue was unveiled in 2021.

Elko was a star player on the 2022 Ole Miss baseball team that won the College World Series. Elko's statue was unveiled in 2024.

title: Justice Department threatens investigation into university professors' BIPOC-only geology camp
description: Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon threatened a probe after a video showed Central Washington University faculty promoting a race-restricted event.
fullText:
Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon threatened a Justice Department investigation into reports of a Black, Indigenous, and People of Color (BIPOC) outdoors camp hosted by public university professors after it faced backlash on Tuesday.

Dhillon responded to a video shared by the Libs of TikTok X account, which appeared to have been deleted from YouTube and other social media, featuring two Central Washington University (CWU) faculty members promoting an upcoming geology retreat that appears to be catering exclusively to a race-restricted minority.

"So is this open to everybody? Not really," CWU senior lecturer Nick Zentner said in the video shared on X, which was edited as evidenced by the abrupt cut-off after he said "not really." "But there's a growing number of people who are younger and are from much more diverse backgrounds who typically don't go to those events for a bunch of reasons. So this is a BIPOC community event."

Trump Admin Wants To Stop Illinois City's Reparations Effort For 'Simply Handing Out Money Based On Race'

CWU assistant professor of geology Hannah Shamloo also promoted the organization hosting the event, the Bronze Chapter, and celebrated its efforts "to increase the participation of BIPOC members in the outdoors."

"Historically, members of BIPOC haven't had the same opportunities for safe engagement with the outdoors, and so Nick and I are here to really extend a warm welcome and encouragement to members of BIPOC to come join us and engage with the geology that we love so much," Shamloo said.

Trump Administration Vows To Stop Reparations Programs, Accuses Officials Of 'Virtue Signaling' To Get 'Votes'

In a comment to Fox News Digital, Central Washington University denied any affiliation with the camp or retreat, though it expressed support for the faculty members involved.

Shamloo and Zentner didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.

"Central Washington University is not affiliated with the nonprofit organization, the Bronze Chapter, and has no direct involvement, financial or otherwise, in the August 21 event that the organization is hosting. However, CWU supports our talented faculty members who volunteer their own time and share their knowledge and expertise with communities outside of CWU," the statement read.

A New York University Faces Justice Department Investigation Over 'Black Male Initiative'

Fox News Digital also reached out to the Bronze Chapter and the Justice Department for comment.

The geology event, called Rock and Role, is scheduled to take place between Aug. 21-23. Though the Bronze Chapter's website does not explicitly restrict people based on race, the event is described as a "POC-centering geology sleepover summer camp" and also provides a BIPOC and Mixed-Race Individual and Family Sponsorship for families of up to ten people.

title: Youngest Black professor at Cambridge resigns as university investigates allegations of plagiarism
description: A British sociologist who became famous as the youngest Black professor ever at the University of Cambridge has resigned after the university opened an investigation into “new information” about his a...
fullText:
LONDON (AP) — A British sociologist who became famous as the youngest Black professor ever at the University of Cambridge has resigned after the university opened an investigation into "new information" about his academic qualifications.

Professor Jason Arday, who was 37 when he became a Cambridge professor in 2023, announced his decision late Wednesday following weeks of allegations about plagiarism in his academic work and questions surrounding claims about his athletic and fundraising accomplishments.

"While criticism is an inevitable part of academic life, what I have experienced has gone far beyond scholarly disagreement," Arday said in a statement. "The relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love."

The statement was distributed by the Good Law Project, a campaign group that has supported Arday since the criticism spilled into the media last month. An earlier letter circulated by the group and signed by more than two dozen academics and politicians described the plagiarism allegations as a "smear campaign" designed to undermine Arday and other Black people who hold "positions of influence."

Arday's appointment at Cambridge highlighted his personal story of overcoming dyslexia, developmental delays and autism that he said left him non-verbal until the age of 11 and illiterate until his late teens.

Questions about his qualifications were raised publicly last month by Nathan Cofnas, a one-time Cambridge philosophy researcher who left the university after his critique of diversity, equity and inclusion programs sparked widespread protests.

On July 24, the Times of London published an analysis of Arday's 2015 Ph.D. thesis highlighting what it said were multiple examples of passages that were "identical or near-identical" to an earlier paper written by another researcher.

The British media also raised questions about Arday's claims that he had raised 5.5 million pounds ($7.4 million) for charity through feats such as running 30 marathons in 35 days and 600 miles in six days.

Arday told the Guardian news website that the money was raised with the help of others over a 20-year period. He said non-disclosure agreements prevented him from naming the others.

Cambridge initially stood by Arday, saying that the plagiarism allegations had been investigated by Liverpool John Moores University, which awarded Arday's doctorate.

That changed Wednesday when Cambridge opened its inquiry.

"The University of Cambridge has begun an investigation following new information about Professor Arday's qualifications and honorary appointments," the university said in a statement. "In order to ensure a fair process, we will not comment further until this has concluded."

The Times of London said Cambridge decided to investigate after it presented new evidence that some of Arday's research was "fabricated" and contained "impossible" evidence.

In an interview with the newspaper published last week, Arday denied plagiarism but admitted to some mistakes that he said were partly due to a lack of supervision when he was working on his doctorate.

Arday continued to defend himself in his resignation statement, saying his decision "should not be interpreted as a loss of faith in scholarship."

"Nor should it be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me'" he said. "It is simply the decision of someone who has reached the limits of what any person should reasonably be expected to endure."

title: Salisbury University announces Justin Axel as new Head Men's Lacrosse Coach
description: Salisbury University has named Justin Axel as the new head coach of their men's lacrosse team.
fullText:
Justin Axel has been hired as Salisbury University's new head men's lacrosse coach, the school announced on Tuesday.

Axel, a Salisbury alum who has served as an assistant coach for the Sea Gulls during two different stints, will be taking over as head coach after longtime head coach Jim Berkman announced his retirement in June.

"This is a special moment for Salisbury men's lacrosse, and Justin is the right person to lead the program forward," Salisbury University Director of Athletics and Campus Recreation Monica Polizzi said in a statement. "He understands what makes Sea Gull lacrosse different because he has helped build its championship tradition for more than a decade. Justin brings championship experience, proven leadership and a deep commitment to developing student-athletes on and off the field. We are confident he will continue the standard of excellence that has made SU one of the premier programs in collegiate lacrosse."

Under Berkman's leadership, Salisbury's men's lacrosse team became one of the premier programs in Division III, winning 13 national titles. Now, Axel will look to continue that success as the new head coach.

"It is a true honor to build upon the incredible legacy of Coach Jim Berkman and Salisbury Men's Lacrosse," Axel said about his hiring. "I am extremely excited about the future of this program and the opportunities that lie ahead. I want to thank President Lepre and Athletic Director Monica Polizzi for this incredible opportunity. Coach Berkman has been an instrumental figure in my life, and I cannot thank him enough for his support, guidance, and friendship over the last 25 years. I am also deeply grateful for the unwavering support of my wife, Meaghan, and my daughter, Sloan—coaching is a family endeavor, and their love and understanding mean everything. I am truly honored to lead this program forward."

Axel first served as an assistant coach for Salisbury from 2002 to 2007, during which the Sea Gulls won four national championships. Axel went on to become the head coach at Eastern Connecticut State in 2007, where his teams recorded an 81-42 record and won four Little East Conference titles during his tenure.

Axel returned to Salisbury in 2014, becoming the recruiting director and assistant coach for the Sea Gulls. Salisbury has won three more national titles since 2014. During their most recent national championship season in 2023, Axel was named the Intercollegiate Men's Lacrosse Coaches Association Division III Assistant Coach of the Year.

title: Mourinho, Ferguson & search for new club - what next for Smalling?
description: Snubbing university, genetics testing for supplements, Sir Alex Ferguson and Jose Mourinho - Chris Smalling is not your ordinary footballer.
fullText:
It is clear from the first answer of a fascinating 45-minute chat that Chris Smalling is no ordinary footballer.

A career that took the 36-year-old from non-league Maidstone to a Champions League final in the space of three years, has, so far, led to 580 club appearances in three countries, playing the majority for Sir Alex Ferguson or Jose Mourinho, plus 31 England caps and trophies with Manchester United and Roma.

It has now brought Smalling and his family back to the north west of England to figure out his next steps.

Smalling has plans for his career after playing but presently, he is focused on finding a new club.

"I know my body now better than when I was 26 and that's shown in the games I'm playing," he said.

"When I was younger, I remember Sir Alex was implementing certain things, like Ryan Giggs doing yoga.

"When you get beyond 30, each year is precious in terms of enjoying playing and being passionate about football.

"Actual training is a very short time. The longevity and recovery starts very early in terms of what I'm eating and doing between sessions, even down to my supplements now.

"In pre-season we have blood tests and the clubs make recommendations. I went one step further and kind of had genetics testing, which goes deep into everything. A lot of my supplements were changed because of that."

Smalling was an ever-present for Al-Fayha in the Saudi Pro-League last season, something he is particularly proud of.

His career is not over. Yet wind back 18 years and Smalling did not imagine he was destined to come anywhere near as far as he has.

"It wasn't even plan D," he recalled.

"I was playing at Maidstone, but I was going to university to study financial economics.

"I had everything set out. I already had my A levels, and I was looking at other non-league clubs near Leicester because I still wanted to play.

"It was very late in the summer when the opportunity came around. I knew it was a slim chance even to be offered but I needed to do everything I could."

The offer was from Fulham. Roy Hodgson watched one practice game, called Smalling into his office and offered a contract.

"It wasn't even a full week," said Smalling. "I didn't have any time to get my head around it. I was just in total shock."

It wouldn't be the last time Hodgson put Smalling into a position where he had no time to think.

He was part of the Fulham squad that travelled to Blackburn for a Premier League game on 17 January, 2010. As it turned out, the then 20-year-old would play no part in the 2-0 defeat.

For him, the important part of the trip took place the previous evening.

"There had been a lot of talk about other clubs but not Manchester United," he said.

"Roy pulled me off the coach, said Fulham had accepted a bid and Sir Alex was coming to the hotel in 45 minutes. I called my mum first but then I was sitting in the room thinking it was going to be a bit awkward and what questions could I can ask him?

"Literally, we were there for about at least a couple of hours. He was so calming and reassuring.

"Even I was doubting it because they had all these great centre-backs. I wanted to develop and wondered 'how do I fit in?'.

"He told me I would get a chance and he believed in me.

"To be able to share the dressing room and the pitch and have conversations with him, is just incredible."

It is that personal side which Smalling feels sets the great managers apart.

To outsiders, his relationship with Mourinho is characterised by a public criticism from the Portuguese in November 2016 around an unwillingness to play through an injury.

That is not how Smalling views it.

"For United or Roma, Jose picked me for most games because we had a good relationship and he trusted me.

"It's very easy to influence younger players but the beauty of Sir Alex and Jose is that they were able to create that belief in senior players. A lot of managers can give good team talks but if you look at some eye-to-eye, see the passion and real belief that 'it's going to happen' senior players follow and the rest lock in. That's the beauty of top-class manager.

"In that situation, I was having injections in broken toe because he had created that mentality in me that I could do anything, even if, maybe, I shouldn't. I had reached the limit of the amount [of injections] I could have, had to stop in a warm-up and he was disappointed.

"It gave me even more belief because it was easy to choose another centre-back but he wanted me."

Smalling remains in contact with Mourinho and wished him good luck when he took over at Real Madrid this summer.

He has no plans to follow his old boss into coaching.

"I don't think it will be my route," he said. "I'm quite comfortable with the next stage.

"I'm working on an education programme for young players partnering with the Global Institute of Sport that's going to be coming out shortly. I've got three or four of these types of projects.

"Once my football career comes to an end, I can put more time to them but at the minute it's all focused on playing because I have that passion and drive and physically my stats are good."

Whoever signs Smalling will get more than just a player.

He had a positive input in Al-Fayha's off-field development, ensuring the gym was suitable for the standards an elite modern-day player demands.

He is proud that at all his previous clubs he is remembered fondly and made a positive impact on and off the pitch.

Turning down that university offer was a good move.

"It would have been the safer route," he said.

"In that first year, I was not earning a lot of money. I was playing for the reserves and the 19th man for the first team, travelling around but not quite on the bench. There was no guarantee I was going to earn more money.

"When I signed for United, it was a four-year contract. At the end of the first year, I signed a new one, another a year later and another 18 months after that.

"There was always this carrot. I never took anything for granted."

fullText:
ESPN has announced the full crew for SEC Nation in 2026, with reporter Marion Crowder rounding out the on-air staff.

Crowder was a soccer star at the University of Georgia from 2013 to 2017, leading the Bulldogs in scoring in three of her four seasons. More recently, she has served as a soccer analyst for ESPN since 2022.

Die-hard hot dog fans may also recognize Crowder, as she's served as ESPN's reporter for the Nathan's Hot Dog Eating Contest.

SEC Nation is effectively SEC Network's version of College GameDay. The show travels to the biggest SEC matchups each Saturday morning during football season.

"I'm incredibly honored to join the SEC Nation team," Crowder said. "This conference has been a part of my life for as long as I can remember. I grew up in a family where Saturdays revolved around SEC football, and I was fortunate enough to experience the conference firsthand as a student-athlete."

ESPN has made a number of changes to SEC Nation this season. Matt Barrie is the new host of the show, replacing Laura Rutledge. Rutledge remains a full-time Monday Night Football sideline reporter and the host of NFL Live.

Chase Daniel is also new to SEC Nation, joining the panel as a replacement for Jordan Rodgers. Rodgers is moving to ESPN's Friday primetime booth alongside Mike Monaco and Dana Boyle.

In addition to Barrie and Daniel, Crowder will also appear alongside established SEC Nation veterans. Paul Finebaum, Roman Harper, and Tim Tebow will all return to the show in 2026 as analysts.

We look back at pass catchers from last year and then forward to Fall as we look ahead.

Some of the high-profile recruiting successes since then (starting in 2022) include Antonio Williams, TJ Moore, Bryant Wesco, Naeem Burroughs, and Jamarin Simmons. WR now figures to be the greatest strength of Clemson's offense. They'll be complemented by a TE room that has two strong options including a senior leader who represented Clemson at ACC Media Days — Olsen Patt-Henry.

75% of the 3,043 of receiving yards from WR/TEs last season will (excluding the 79 yards from Ian Schieffelin and former walk-ons) is back next season.

TJ Moore is a true star. He is an extremely well-rounded athlete measuring in at 6-3 200lbs. He has the size and strength to win jump balls, the speed to get separation, the agility to get open in small spaces and avoid tackles, and great hands to make it all count. Let's look at a few highlights. In this first one we see his acceleration and shiftiness, and he makes an LSU defender miss:

On this screen you see his acceleration turn a modest gain into a TD.

Finally, appreciate the hands on this catch. Christopher Vizzina slightly overthrows this ball, but it's no problem for an elite wide receiver.

Bryant Wesco is the other first round caliber talent we must highlight. He is coming off a back/neck injury sustained on a punt return but appears to be healthy entering Fall. He averaged 17.3 yards per reception in both 2024 and 2025. He has the speed to get open and the size and ball skills to win with the ball in the air. Here he demonstrates those ball skills.

Here he is using his speed and vision to navigate through defenders and turn a nice 15-yard gain on a dig route into a long TD.

Of course, we can't show Bryant Wesco film without showing his first career TD because it was so memorable. Clemson fans were so desperate for explosiveness after Georgia shut them down. Wesco provided it on the first drive after sitting on the bench for most of the season opener vs. Georgia.

I've always thought of Wesco as the taller, lankier of the two superstar receivers — almost like Martavis Bryant— but they're actually about the same size (in fact Wesco is listed as 1 inch shorter and 5 lbs lighter than Moore). Wesco proved to have the agility to make defenders miss in small spaces which is why the staff put him at punt returner. I still don't love him there and would prefer a slot receiver in that role, but Wesco has proven to be a do-it-all type just like TJ Moore.

Tyler Brown had a great freshman campaign in 2023, was injured in 2024, and then never really made a mark on the 2025 season despite being healthy. He was getting a lot of hype and praise coming into the year, but it never materialized. He has a chance to earn and hold a starting WR spot in the slot, but he needs to avoid costly drops.

Tristan Smith seemed underutilized for much of the year, but when injuries forced him into action, he had a bad case of the drops too. He sued and won for a 5th year of eligibility, and he should be a great backup for the stars (Moore/Wesco) on the outside.

At tight end, Clemson boasts a solid duo of Olsen Patt-Henry and Christian Betancur. Betancur is the better receiver who came in as an extremely highly rated prospect. If he can improve his blocking, he can be an NFL draft candidate. Patt-Henry has missed each of the last two springs with injuries. This time it was a knee injury sustained last November. Despite that, he is a team leader and will get plenty of snaps. PFF graded him poorly, but I remain high on what he brings to the offense as a well-rounded TE. Chad Morris has traditionally used the TEs more than what we saw last year so it would not be shocking to see this duo exceed the 341 combined yards they had last season.

While Clemson returns 75% of the production at WR/TE, they still lose Antonio Williams which leaves a big void to fill. Fortunately, these five newcomers plus improved health from Bryant Wesco can help fill that void.

WR Naeem Burroughs: No. 11 WR recruit nationally. Hails from Jacksonville, FL. 5-11 185lbs and will battle Tyler Brown for snaps in the slot. I expect him to push Brown for snaps.

At 6-3 200lbs, he has the same build as TJ Moore. He was the no. 27 wide receiver nationally and hails from Charlotte, NC.

WR Connor Salmin: No. 30 WR nationally. Hails from Maryland. A speedster who has posted a stellar 10.44 100-meter dash time.

TE Tayveon Wilson: 3-star from West Virginia, but had offers from Miami, Louisville, Penn State, and Virginia Tech. Played multiple sports in high school including being a standout baseball player. Redshirting no longer exists, but he may de facto redshirt as he focuses on playing tight end. Will need to add some muscle to block at the position.

Only 5-10 165 according to 247 and missed most of senior year with a high ankle sprain. Had another P4 offer from Louisville. Could be an example of a player who is better than the typical walk-on, but not someone we would have signed to a full scholarship with the old 85-man scholarship limit. Probably a good use of a roster spot in the new world.

There are major questions on this offense including a quarterback (Christopher Vizzina) with just one career start and an offensive line that has only two players who played at least 125 offensive snaps and posted a PFF grade of 65.0 or better (Brayden Jacobs and Ronan O'Connell). Wide Receiver and Tight End are major strengths though. They have the talent to erase slightly off target throws and turn 15-yard plays into 50-yard plays. If the offensive line and QB are passable, the pass catchers can make them look far better than that.

title: Attorney who defended DC sniper says Kohberger faces 'monumental uphill battle' undoing guilty plea
description: A criminal defense attorney explains why Bryan Kohberger's effort to undo his University of Idaho murders guilty plea faces two significant legal hurdles.
fullText:
Bryan Kohberger faces a "monumental uphill battle" in his effort to withdraw his guilty plea in the murders of four University of Idaho students, according to an attorney who represented D.C. sniper Lee Boyd Malvo and once helped another client successfully withdraw a guilty plea before winning an acquittal.

Mark Petrovich, who represented Malvo in post-conviction proceedings in Virginia and has decades of criminal defense experience, told Fox News Digital that defendants rarely succeed in withdrawing guilty pleas after sentencing, even in cases involving claims that they were unaware of potentially exculpatory evidence before entering the plea.

He cautioned against drawing direct comparisons between Malvo's post-conviction litigation and Kohberger's effort to withdraw his guilty plea. Malvo's appeals stemmed from changes in constitutional law governing juvenile sentencing, while Kohberger is attempting to undo a plea agreement he entered as an adult after avoiding the death penalty.

Kaylee Goncalves' Mother Says Family Ready For Trial After Bryan Kohberger Seeks To Withdraw Guilty Plea

"It's a monumental uphill battle," Petrovich said. "First of all, getting the judge to allow you to withdraw the plea, and then second of all to winning any new proceeding, because there's a lot against you."

Kohberger pleaded guilty in July 2025 to the stabbing deaths of University of Idaho students Ethan Chapin, Xana Kernodle, Madison Mogen and Kaylee Goncalves in Moscow, Idaho, in November 2022. He was sentenced to four consecutive life sentences without the possibility of parole after accepting a plea agreement that spared him from the death penalty.

Follow The Fox True Crime Team On X

In recent court filings, Kohberger claimed he was pressured into accepting the plea agreement, did not fully understand potentially exculpatory evidence before pleading guilty and was misled about the conditions he would face while incarcerated.

Idaho Murders: New Book On Kohberger Reveals Previously Unseen Evidence, Claims Sheath Could Be Inadmissible

He contends those factors undermined the voluntariness of his decision to plead guilty.

Petrovich said he once represented a client who sought to withdraw a guilty plea before sentencing. A judge granted the request, the case proceeded to trial and the client was acquitted, but he said Kohberger's circumstances are fundamentally different because he has already been sentenced.

"You can't wait until after you're sentenced and see what the consequences of the plea are and then change your plea," Petrovich said. "It's going to be a very, very difficult burden to overcome."

Alex Murdaugh Murder Saga Lands Right Back Where It Started Before Next Lowcountry Courtroom Battle

Petrovich said Kohberger would face two significant hurdles even if a judge allowed him to withdraw his plea.

One would be convincing jurors after previously admitting guilt under oath.

Like What You're Reading? Click Here For More

Even if a judge allowed Kohberger to withdraw his plea, Petrovich said jurors would almost certainly learn he had already admitted guilt, creating another significant obstacle at trial.

"One thing that's important is that you still can't hide from the jury the fact that you said under oath that you're guilty," Petrovich said. "Even if you withdraw, then you have to explain that ... if you're going to get anywhere with any kind of jury finding."

Petrovich also questioned whether Kohberger's attorneys would have advised him to accept a plea agreement without first reviewing the evidence disclosed during discovery.

He noted that defense attorneys handling capital cases typically spend years reviewing discovery before recommending whether a client should plead guilty.

"The attorneys on the case ... were intimately familiar with the evidence and the information that was provided to them by law enforcement and prosecution," Petrovich said. "I'm sure they knew all about everything. If they encouraged him or if there was a discussion and a plea was decided on, I'm sure it was for good reason."

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Kohberger's case is not the first involving a notorious killer who later sought to undo a guilty plea.

James Earl Ray pleaded guilty in 1969 to assassinating the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. to avoid a potential death sentence. Three days after entering his guilty plea, Ray sought to withdraw it, arguing he had been pressured into confessing. He spent the rest of his life trying to undo the plea but died in prison in 1998 without ever receiving the jury trial he sought.

Serial killer Clifton Bloomfield unsuccessfully sought to withdraw guilty pleas after admitting to five murders in New Mexico to avoid capital punishment. Washington serial killer Robert Lee Yates Jr. also challenged his plea agreement after admitting to murdering 13 women, but courts ultimately rejected both efforts.

Kohberger's plea agreement spared him from facing a capital trial and ended years of pretrial litigation in one of the country's most closely watched murder prosecutions.

Petrovich said that history, combined with the years of discovery and plea negotiations leading up to Kohberger's agreement, makes the effort to withdraw it especially difficult.
